Scope

3

Definitions

This International Standard specifies a format and recording standard for 9-track, 12,7 mm (0,5 in) magnetic tape to be used for data interchange between information processing systems, communication systems, and associated equipment utilizing the 7-bit coded character set (see ISO W), its extension in ISO 2022 where required, and the 8-bit coded character sat (see ISO W3). Magnetic Iabelling for use on magnetic tape is the subject of ISO 1~1. The magnetic tape and reel to be used shall conform to ISO lW and/or ISO ~.
NOTE � Numeric values in the S1 and/or Imparisl measurement system in this International Standard may have bean rounded off and therefore are consistent with, but not exactly qual to, each other. Either system may be used, but the two shouldbe neitherintermixed nor reconverted. Tha original design was made using the Imperial measurement system.

For the purpose of this International Standard, the following definitions apply. 3.1 magnetic tape: A tape which will accept and retain magnetic signals intended for input, output and storage purposes on computers and associatedequipment.

3.2

reference tape: A tape which has bean selected for given properties for use in calibration. Master Standard Reference Tape: A reference tape selected as a standard for signal amplitude.
NOTE � A Master Standard Reference Tape has been aatsbhshed by the US National Institute for Standards and Technology (NIST}.

The average flux transition spacing shall be within * 3 % of 31,75 wm (1 250 win). This average shall be measured over a minimum of 1,2 x l@ successive flux transitions, at the extremes of operating conditions, by reading a tape that has been continuously and evenlv recorded at 31,5 ftpmm (~ ftpi) in phase in all tracks.

5.4

Instantaneous flux transition spacing

The in-ntsnwus spacing between flux transitions msv be influenced bv the reading and writing processes, the pattern recorded (pulse crowding effects) and other factors. Messuremsnts are taken from leading edge to leading edge of flux transition. The following conditions shall all be met. a) The spacing between the first detected bits of eucceesive rows shall be greater than 22,9 Km (600 pin); b) The spacing between the first detected bmand the kst detected bit of a rowshsll be 1sssthan 10,8pm (=.pin); c) There shell be a minimum apparent spacing between anv bite of successive rows of 11,2 pm (440 pin).

Recording
Method of recording

The average peek-to-peek output signal amptitude of an interchanged tape at 32 ftpmm (600 ftpi) shall be between 70 % and 115 % of the Standard Reference Amptitude. Averaging shall be done over a minimum of 4000 flux transitions which, for the interchange tape, may be segmented into blocks. Averaging shall be done on the first md pass after interchange. 5.6.3 Maximum signal amplitude

The "non return to zero chen~n-ones recording" (NRZ1 ) method of recording shall be used where a ONE is represented bv a change of direction of kngitudnal magnetization.

An interchanged tape shall contain no flux transition the bto-peek signal amptitude of which exceeds 120 % of on~hsti the Standard Reference Amptitude on the first read pass after interchange.

Quality of recording for data interchange

15 mm nom. (0,6 in nom. ) 12,7 mm min. (0,5 in min.) 7600 mm max. (300 in max.).

Tape shall not be used for data interchange where the number of gaps which have been elongated due to erase instructions exceed two in number or 0,5 % of the total number of blocks written, whichever is the larger. No permanent parity errors whilst writing are permissible in the data to be interchanged.

This gap shall be erased in accordance

with 5.7. The actual gap length depends on the number of consecutive erase instructions.

CRC gap

10 Erasure of lD bursts
The use of tapes recorded at 63 cpmm (1 ~ cpi) and 2W cpmm (6 250 cpi) for recording at 32 cpmm (600 cpi) presents a difficulty in that the identification burst on such a tape extends from a minimum of 43,2 mm (.1,7 in) before the trailing edge of the .BOT marker. To ensure proper working of the 32 cpmm (800 cpi) system, it is necessaw for the burst to"be erased, either by the system itself or by bulk erasure.

Annex A
(normative)

CRC register

A.1

Generation

ragkter to be Cl to Cg Consider the contents of a $~.tion with the following track assignments: Register postiron: Cl C2 C3 Ca C5 C6 C7 Ca Cg Track numhr: 476539182

To determine whether the errors occurred in a single track, and if so, whkh, an error pattern (EP) must be generated. This pa~em must then be compared with the error indicating pattern in the CRC register. Consider the contents of a 9-position EP register to be El to Eg corresponding to Cl to Cg of the CRC register. The error pattern may be constructed as follows: a) whenever a character parity error is detected for a data character or for the CRC character, a ONE is added without carry to Eg (exclusive OR); b) between the reading of characters, the EP register is shifted by one position: & to E2, etc., and Eg to El; c) if shifting w.11cause El to contain ONE, then-the bits being shifted into positions E&E& E6 and E7 are inverted. To determine thelrack in error, a series of comparisonsis made between -the contents of the EP register and the CRC register. The CRC register, read out through the mask which inve~ all positions axcept C4 and CGis compared with the EP register. The first comparison is direct: El to Cl, E2 to C2, etc. If all positions match, the error was in the track associated with Cg (track 2). Tha CRC register is then shifted once, according to A.1 b) and A.1 c) between each comparison. This is continued until a match is obtained or until a maximum of nine comparisons (eight shifts) have bean made. The track in error cormponds to Cg through Cl for a match on the first through ninth comparison respectively. There are two conditions for the final contents of the CRC register for which an uncorrectable error has been detected and for which an incorrect track-in-error indication will be obtained if comparisons are made. These are as follows: a) Cl to Cg contain ZEROS;

The CRC character shall be derived as follows: a) all data rows in the block are added to the CRC register without carry (excluaiva OR); b) between additions, the CRC register& ahti position: Cl to C2, etc., and Cg to Cl; by one

c) if shting will cause Cl to contain ONE, then the bits being shtid into positions C* C& C& and C, are inverted; d) after the bits of last data character have bean added, if shfing will cause Cl to become ONE, then the C-RCregister is shfiad once more in accordance with b) and c); e) to write the CRC character on tape, the contents of all positions except C4 and C6 are inve~ad. The parity of tha CRC character will be odd if the number of data characters within the block is even, and even if the number of data characters within the block is odd. The CRC character may contain on~ ZEROS, in which case the number of data characters is odd.

A.2

CRC register

When reading, the CRC register is controlled as it was for writing until the bst data character has bean added and the final shift made. The CRC character on tape is then added to the ragi%r. To test for an error, the register is reed out inverting all positions except C4 and~8 If the masked output of any position is a ONE, an error has bean detected.

b) C4 to CGcontain ZEROS, all other positions containing ONES (the reed-out mask). If a track-in-error indication is obtained, the error block maybe ra-md. The output of the track in error is then inverted whenever the parity of a character is incorrect.

Annex C
(informative)

Storage and transportation

C.1

Environment
the

It is recommended that during storage and transpo~tion tapes are kept within the following conditions: temperature: 5 `C to 32 `C (~�F relative humidity: ~ % to ~ % to W `F)

d) The final box should have a clean interior and a lid construction that provides sufficient seating to prevent the ingress of dirt and water. e) The orientation of the reals within the final box should be such that their axes amhonzontal. f) The final box should be clearly marked to indicate its correct otiantation.

wet bulb temperature: not greater than ~ `C (W `F) There shall be no condensation on the tape. C.2.2 Extremes of temperature and humidity

C.2

Hazards
of data-bearing magnetic tape invohes three

Those extremes which could set up stresses within the body of the tape. Recommendations a) Extreme changes in temperature and humidity should b-avoided wherever possible. b) When a tape is received it should be conditioned in the operating environment (sea 4.1 ) for a period of 2 h to 12 h depending upon the extent of exposure to conditions outside the operating environment.

Transportation

basic potential hazards:

C.2.1 Impact loads and vibrations during transportation
Those forces which could cause damage to the reel, or movement within the tape pack, with consequential loss of wind tension. Recommendations a) The free end of the tape should be secured to prevent any tendency to unwind. b) A rigid plastic container free from dust or other extraneous matter should be used. c) The plastic container(s) should be fitted into a rigid box containing adequate shock absotint material.

C.2.3

Effects of stray magnetic field

Those effects which would possibly cause corruption of data.

Recommendation
A nominal spacing of not leas than ~ mm (3,15 in) should exist between the magnetic tape reel and the outer surface of the final container, in which case it is considered that the risk of corruption will be negligible.
